summary: This document extends the IMAP SEARCH and UID SEARCH commands with result options controlling what is returned, namely the minimal value, the maximal value, all matches and the count of matches. It was later updated by RFC 9394.

plainLanguage.summary: This IMAP extension lets a client choose what a search returns. It can ask for the lowest match, the highest match, all matching identifiers or just the count.

questions: how do i get the first unseen message in imap
what does search return count do in imap
subtitle: Lets IMAP clients request selected search results instead of every matching message number.

tldr.problem: A normal IMAP search can return every matching message number, even when a client only needs one result or a count.
tldr.mechanism: The RETURN options MIN, MAX, ALL and COUNT specify what to include in an ESEARCH response.
tldr.outcome: Clients can request a smaller or more useful result. RFC 9394 later updates this extension.

today: RFC 4731 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9394.

sections.title: Choosing What a Search Returns
sections.content:
RFC 4731 extends IMAP SEARCH and UID SEARCH with result options. A server that advertises the ESEARCH capability supports the extension. The options can save bandwidth when a client needs only a summary of the matches.

For example, a client can request the first unseen message or the number of deleted messages. A server may also optimize a search that asks only for MIN or MAX.
sections.plainLanguage: A search does not always need to return a long list. The client can ask for the specific result it needs.

sections.title: The Four Result Options
sections.content:
MIN returns the lowest matching message number or UID, and MAX returns the highest. ALL returns every match using sequence-set syntax; clients must not assume a particular order. COUNT returns the number of matching messages and must always appear in the response.

If no messages match, the server omits MIN, MAX and ALL but still sends ESEARCH. An empty option list is equivalent to requesting ALL.
sections.plainLanguage: MIN and MAX return one end of the matching range. ALL returns the matching identifiers, while COUNT returns how many messages matched.

sections.title: The ESEARCH Response
sections.content:
When an extended SEARCH requests one or more result options, the server must send one ESEARCH response instead of the usual SEARCH response. An extended UID SEARCH includes a UID indicator, so the returned values refer to UIDs.

The response carries the requested result data and identifies the command it answers. The RFC includes examples of requesting MIN with COUNT, requesting ALL, and finding the first unseen message.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends an ESEARCH response with the selected result values. For UID SEARCH, the response marks the values as UIDs.

sections.title: Using ESEARCH with CONDSTORE
sections.content:
When a server supports both ESEARCH and CONDSTORE, and a search includes MODSEQ with a result option, it must use ESEARCH and include the MODSEQ result. The value represents the relevant modification sequence for the returned messages.

For a single MIN or MAX, MODSEQ belongs to that message. Other combinations use the highest modification sequence among the messages being returned, as specified by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: When a search also asks about message changes, the answer includes a change value. Which messages determine that value depends on the requested results.

sections.title: Security and Capability Registration
sections.content:
IMAP searches can require substantial processor and disk work, so some servers disable them as a possible denial-of-service risk. ALL and COUNT change the returned information, not the search itself; MIN and MAX may reduce work when a server optimizes them.

The RFC says the extension adds no security concerns beyond those already discussed for IMAP. IANA added ESEARCH to the IMAP capabilities registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Search can be costly for a server. Returning fewer results does not usually change the search work, though MIN or MAX can help an optimizing server.
